advisories.summary: Command WebSocket buffers unbounded messages before checking permissions
advisories.description:
## Summary

The `/api/command` WebSocket handler reads a complete client message before checking either
`EnableExec` or the user's `Perm.Execute` permission, and never calls `SetReadLimit`. Any authenticated
user who can reach the endpoint — including one with no command-execution permission, on a server where
the command feature is disabled — can make the process allocate and retain an arbitrarily large
WebSocket message before the request is rejected.

Verified at v2.63.23, the final release. The handler has had this shape since v2.0.0.

## Details

`commandsHandler` upgrades the connection and reads a full message before any authorization check:

```go
// http/commands.go:41-68
var commandsHandler = withUser(func(w http.ResponseWriter, r *http.Request, d *data) (int, error) {
	conn, err := upgrader.Upgrade(w, r, nil)
	...
	for {
		_, msg, err := conn.ReadMessage()
		...
		raw = strings.TrimSpace(string(msg))
		if raw != "" {
			break
		}
	}

	// Fail fast
	if !d.server.EnableExec || !d.user.Perm.Execute {
```

No `conn.SetReadLimit` call occurs anywhere in the codebase, and gorilla/websocket applies no default
bound: its size guard is `if c.readLimit > 0 && c.readLength > c.readLimit` (`conn.go:924`), so the
zero-value limit disables the check entirely. `ReadMessage` then buffers the whole message with
`ioutil.ReadAll` (`conn.go:1091-1099`). The `ReadBufferSize: 1024` on the upgrader
(`http/commands.go:22-25`) sizes the underlying read buffer only; it does not bound the assembled
message. `string(msg)` copies the buffer a second time before the comparison.

The route is registered unconditionally, so disabling the command feature does not remove it:

```go
// http/http.go:88
api.PathPrefix("/command").Handler(monkey(commandsHandler, "/api/command")).Methods("GET")
```

`commandsHandler` is the only WebSocket handler in the codebase; the other endpoints are plain HTTP and
the JSON auth routes are already bounded by `maxAuthBodySize` (`http/auth.go:24,159,193`).

## PoC

Against revision `833d9088`, as a user with empty permissions and a server built with
`EnableExec: false`, a 32 MiB message is fully buffered before the handler answers
`Command not allowed.`:

```go
payload := bytes.Repeat([]byte("A"), 32<<20)
if err := conn.WriteMessage(websocket.TextMessage, payload); err != nil {
	t.Fatal(err)
}

_, response, err := conn.ReadMessage()
// → "Command not allowed."
```

```bash
GOTOOLCHAIN=local go test ./http -run '^TestPOCCommandWebSocketUnboundedMessage$' -count=2 -v
```

The reporter's proof is bounded at 32 MiB and local-only; nothing in the handler imposes that bound.

## Impact

Any authenticated user can drive the server's heap with a single connection, regardless of whether they
hold `Perm.Execute` and regardless of whether `EnableExec` is set, because the rejection happens only
after the message has been read in full. Repeated or concurrent connections make the process
unresponsive or terminate it under ordinary container and host memory limits. Confidentiality and
integrity of stored files are not affected.

## Patches

None. The project is no longer maintained and no fix will ship.

## Workarounds

- Block `/api/command` at the reverse proxy unless the command feature is actually in use. The endpoint
  has no other purpose, and its route is registered even when `EnableExec` is false, so denying the path
  (or refusing WebSocket upgrades to it) removes the exposure without affecting anything else.
- Run File Browser under a memory limit with a restart policy, so an exhausted process is contained and
  recovered rather than taking the host with it.

## Out of scope

Command execution itself, the runner and the command allowlist. The reporter explicitly did not claim
execution or an allowlist bypass, and this advisory makes no claim about them either. That class is
known, unaddressed, and tracked separately in
[#5199](https://github.com/filebrowser/filebrowser/issues/5199).

## References

- GHSA-w5fm-68j4-fpc4 — DoS on the public login API; its fix introduced the `maxAuthBodySize` bound that
  the WebSocket path has no equivalent of.
- [#5199](https://github.com/filebrowser/filebrowser/issues/5199) — command execution, runner and hooks.

advisories.summary: Subtitle conversion reads whole files into memory, allowing memory exhaustion
advisories.description:
## Summary

The subtitle endpoint converts `.srt`, `.ass` and `.ssa` files to WebVTT by loading them into memory in full, with no size limit anywhere on the path. An authenticated user can request conversion of a large subtitle file and make the server allocate several times its size; concurrent requests exhaust memory and terminate the process. The 10 MB cap that bounds the text-content read path does not apply here, because the subtitle handler never asks for file content and so never reaches that check. Reported against v2.63.23 and verified at v2.63.23.

## Details

`subtitleHandler` in `http/subtitle.go` resolves the file with `files.NewFileInfo` leaving `Content` unset. `detectType` therefore takes no content-reading branch, and its size check —

```go
	case (strings.HasPrefix(mimetype, "text") || !isBinary(buffer)) && i.Size <= 10*1024*1024: // 10 MB
```

— never constrains what follows. `subtitleFileHandler` then opens the file itself and reads all of it:

```go
	if strings.HasSuffix(file.Name, ".srt") {
		content, readErr := io.ReadAll(fd)
		if readErr != nil {
			return http.StatusInternalServerError, readErr
		}
		sub, err = astisub.ReadFromSRT(bytes.NewReader(normalizeSRTLineBreaks(content)))
	} else if strings.HasSuffix(file.Name, ".ass") || strings.HasSuffix(file.Name, ".ssa") {
		sub, err = astisub.ReadFromSSA(fd)
	}
```

For an N-byte `.srt` the handler holds the `io.ReadAll` buffer, a second full copy produced by `normalizeSRTLineBreaks` — `regexp.ReplaceAll` returns a new slice — and the parsed `astisub.Subtitles` structure, before `WriteToWebVTT` renders the result into a third buffer. Peak usage is a multiple of the file size. The `.ass`/`.ssa` branch streams the descriptor rather than buffering it, but `astisub.ReadFromSSA` still builds an in-memory structure proportional to the input, so it is unbounded too.

Two distinct phases are worth separating. The unbounded parse has existed since the subtitle feature shipped in v2.0.0. The `io.ReadAll` call and the extra full copy were added in v2.63.17, by the fix preserving SRT line breaks, which raised the multiplier on the `.srt` path.

The endpoint is authenticated only. `/api/subtitle` is registered on the authenticated router in `http/http.go`, and no public-share route reaches `subtitleFileHandler` — `publicDlHandler` serves through `rawFileHandler`, which streams.

## PoC

Preconditions: an authenticated account with `Perm.Download`, and a large subtitle file within its scope. `Perm.Create` lets the attacker supply one; otherwise any sufficiently large existing `.srt` will do.

1. Authenticate against `POST /api/login` and keep the token.
2. Upload a large `.srt`:

   ```http
   POST /api/resources/dos.srt?override=true HTTP/1.1
   Host: TARGET
   X-Auth: <token>
   Content-Type: application/octet-stream

   <a few tens of MB of SRT text>
   ```

3. Request the conversion:

   ```http
   GET /api/subtitle/dos.srt HTTP/1.1
   Host: TARGET
   X-Auth: <token>
   ```

The server reads the file in full and allocates a multiple of its size. Issuing the request repeatedly and concurrently drives resident memory up until the process is killed.

## Impact

An authenticated user with download permission can exhaust the server's memory and terminate it, denying service to every user of the instance. In containers with a memory limit the process is killed promptly; without one it can starve the host. Confidentiality and integrity are unaffected.

## Patches

None. The project is no longer maintained and no fix will ship.

## Workarounds

- Withhold `Perm.Create` from untrusted accounts so they cannot place a large subtitle file, and check existing scopes for oversized `.srt`, `.ass` and `.ssa` files. Download permission alone is not enough to exploit this if no such file exists.
- Run File Browser with a memory limit and automatic restart, so a successful attack costs an instance restart rather than the host.
- Where a reverse proxy fronts File Browser, rate-limit `GET /api/subtitle/` per account.

## Out of scope

The report presents this as a bypass of the CVE-2025-53893 patch. It is not, and the advisory does not describe it that way:

- The 10 MB cap in `files/file.go` was not introduced by a fix for CVE-2025-53893. It arrived in v2.12.0, released in 2021, several years before that report, and GHSA-7xqm-7738-642x shipped with no patched version at all.
- The subtitle path was never covered by that cap, so there is no incomplete fix here. This is a separate unbounded sink on a different endpoint, and it is treated as its own defect.

## References

- Earlier unbounded-read report on the text-content path: GHSA-7xqm-7738-642x
- Size check that bounds the text-content path and not this one: `files/file.go`, `detectType`

advisories.summary: Upload failure-cleanup recursively deletes directories, bypassing Perm.Delete and deny rules
advisories.description:
## Summary

The direct-upload endpoint removes its target on a failed write, but never rejects a target that is an existing directory. A `POST` with `?override=true` aimed at a directory therefore fails inside `writeFile` — a directory cannot be opened for writing — and the failure cleanup then runs `RemoveAll` on the request path, recursively destroying the whole tree. The cleanup is gated by neither `Perm.Delete` nor the descendant rule walk, so an authenticated user holding only the default Create and Modify permissions can delete directories they are not allowed to delete, including rule-denied files inside them. Reported against v2.63.23 and verified at v2.63.23.

## Details

`resourcePostHandler` in `http/resource.go` authorizes the upload with `Perm.Create` and a rule check on the request path, then resolves the target:

```go
	file, err := files.NewFileInfo(&files.FileOptions{...})
	if err == nil {
		if r.URL.Query().Get("override") != "true" {
			return http.StatusConflict, nil
		}

		// Permission for overwriting the file
		if !d.user.Perm.Modify {
			return http.StatusForbidden, nil
		}
		...
	}
```

`NewFileInfo` succeeds for an existing directory, and unlike `tusPostHandler` — which rejects one explicitly:

```go
		if file != nil {
			if file.IsDir {
				return http.StatusBadRequest, fmt.Errorf("cannot upload to a directory %s", file.RealPath())
			}
```

— this handler has no `file.IsDir` guard. Execution falls through to `writeFile`, whose `OpenFile(dst, os.O_RDWR|os.O_CREATE|os.O_TRUNC, fileMode)` always fails on a directory (`is a directory` on Linux, `Access is denied` on Windows). The failure path then removes the target:

```go
	if err != nil {
		_ = d.user.Fs.RemoveAll(r.URL.Path)
	}
```

`RemoveAll` recurses. Two authorization checks that the delete and patch handlers apply are absent here:

- `Perm.Delete`, enforced by `resourceDeleteHandler`;
- `checkDescendants`, added to `resourceDeleteHandler` and `resourcePatchHandler` for GHSA-77x8-73f4-5485, which walks the subtree and refuses the operation if a rule denies any path inside it.

`ScopedFs.RemoveAll` does call `guard`, so the deletion cannot leave the user's scope — that is the fix for GHSA-fmm7-x4gx-8jhr, and it holds. `guard` proves containment only; it says nothing about the permission bits, the rules, or whether the target is a directory.

The cleanup was introduced in v2.5.0. A later fix, v2.16.0, removed the equivalent cleanup from `resourcePutHandler` but left the one in the upload path.

## PoC

Preconditions: an authenticated non-administrator with `create=true` and `modify=true` — the default preset — and `delete=false`.

```bash
# user "guest": perm.delete=false
JWT=$(curl -s -X POST http://127.0.0.1:8333/api/login \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d '{"username":"guest","password":"…"}')

mkdir -p srv/shared/team && echo data > srv/shared/team/plan.txt

# 1) the delete endpoint correctly refuses
curl -o /dev/null -w '%{http_code}\n' -X DELETE \
  http://127.0.0.1:8333/api/resources/shared/team -H "X-Auth: $JWT"
# -> 403

# 2) one upload request wipes the tree
curl -o /dev/null -w '%{http_code}\n' -X POST \
  'http://127.0.0.1:8333/api/resources/shared/team?override=true' \
  -H "X-Auth: $JWT" --data-binary x
# -> 500 ; srv/shared/team and its whole subtree are gone
```

The server log shows the root cause: `POST /shared/team -> 500 … open <root>/shared/team: is a directory`.

The rule variant behaves the same way. With a global rule denying `/important2/secret.txt`, a direct `GET` or `DELETE` of that file returns `403`, but `POST /api/resources/important2?override=true` deletes the entire `important2` tree, the rule-denied file included.

Both results reproduce against the real handlers with the delete-permission and deny-rule negative controls in place: `DELETE /team` returns `403` and `POST /team/sub/secret.txt?override=true` returns `403`, while `POST /team?override=true` returns `500` and removes the tree.

## Impact

An authenticated user with the default Create and Modify permissions can permanently delete any directory inside their scope with a single request, with no trash and no undo.

- **`Perm.Delete` bypass.** Accounts deliberately granted upload-only access — create and modify, without delete — can destroy arbitrary directory trees.
- **Deny-rule bypass.** Files protected by a rule are destroyed along with an allowed parent, the same class of failure as GHSA-77x8-73f4-5485 but through a handler that fix did not cover.
- **Shared scopes.** Where several users share a scope, a restricted account can delete other users' data.

Confidentiality is unaffected: the write is refused and nothing is disclosed.

## Patches

None. The project is no longer maintained and no fix will ship.

## Workarounds

There is no configuration that closes this while leaving uploads usable, because the affected request is an ordinary upload.

- Withhold `Perm.Modify` from accounts that do not need to overwrite files. Without it the override branch returns `403` before reaching `writeFile`, and the cleanup is never reached.
- Where a reverse proxy sits in front of File Browser, reject `POST` requests to `/api/resources/…` carrying `override=true` whose path has no file extension, or restrict them to trusted accounts. This is a heuristic, not a boundary.
- Keep backups. The deletion is immediate and unrecoverable from within File Browser.

## References

- Descendant rule walk that this handler does not use: GHSA-77x8-73f4-5485
- Scope containment on the same cleanup call, fixed and still holding: GHSA-fmm7-x4gx-8jhr
- Directory rejection this handler is missing, as implemented for TUS uploads: `http/tus_handlers.go`

advisories.summary: Symlink aliases inside a user scope bypass path deny rules
advisories.description:
## Summary

File Browser authorizes a request against the normalized lexical path it was asked for, while `ScopedFs` later resolves symbolic links to prove the target stays inside the user's scope. Nothing reapplies the path rules to the resolved target. Where a symbolic link inside an allowed directory points at a rule-denied object, and both ends stay inside the user's scope, an authenticated non-administrator can read and overwrite files a rule was written to protect by addressing them through the link. Reported against v2.63.23 and verified at v2.63.23; the same source-to-sink shape is present in every v2 release.

## Details

The rule decision and the filesystem access operate on different names.

`data.CheckRules` in `http/data.go` matches the requested virtual path against the global and per-user rule sets:

```go
	allow := true
	for _, rule := range d.settings.Rules {
		if rule.Matches(path, d.server.CaseInsensitiveFs) {
			allow = rule.Allow
		}
	}
```

and `Rule.Matches` in `rules/rules.go` is purely lexical — a regex match, or a case-aware path-prefix comparison:

```go
	prefix := rulePath
	if prefix != "/" && !strings.HasSuffix(prefix, "/") {
		prefix += "/"
	}

	return strings.HasPrefix(path, prefix)
```

A rule denying `/denied` does not match `/allowed/link`, so the request is authorized. The filesystem layer then resolves the link. `ScopedFs.within` in `files/scoped.go` calls `filepath.EvalSymlinks` and accepts the target if it remains under the scoped root:

```go
	return resolved == root || strings.HasPrefix(resolved, prefix), nil
```

`within` has no access to the rule sets. It answers "is this object inside the scope?", which is a different question from "do the rules allow this object?". Both reads and writes reach the resolved target with the rules applied only to the alias:

- `rawHandler` (`http/raw.go`) requires `Perm.Download`, passes `r.URL.Path` to `files.NewFileInfo`, whose `Checker.Check` runs before any stat or open, and then serves the opened file.
- `resourcePutHandler` (`http/resource.go`) requires `Perm.Modify`, calls `d.Check(r.URL.Path)`, and then hands the path to `writeFile`, which opens it `O_RDWR|O_CREATE|O_TRUNC` and copies the request body in.

The mismatch is:

```text
checked lexical path:      /allowed/link/overwrite.txt
resolved physical target:  /denied/overwrite.txt
rule applied to target:    no
```

The rule-check architecture dates to the initial v2 release, and no version has rechecked the resolved target.

## PoC

Preconditions: a symbolic link on an allowed path already resolves to a rule-denied object, and both the link and its target are inside the user's scope. File Browser exposes no API that creates such a link, so it arrives out of band — an administrator-created layout, a mounted or shared volume, a restored backup, or an extracted archive.

The tested attacker is an authenticated non-administrator scoped to `/srv` with `Download` and `Modify` and nothing else — no `Create`, `Rename`, `Delete`, `Share`, `Execute` or `Admin`. A global non-regex prefix rule denies `/denied`. The directory link `/allowed/link -> ../denied` exists before the server starts.

Only the request path changes between the control and the attack:

```text
GET /api/raw/denied/secret.txt              -> 403
GET /api/raw/allowed/link/secret.txt        -> 200, full file contents returned

PUT /api/resources/denied/overwrite.txt     -> 403
PUT /api/resources/allowed/link/overwrite.txt -> 200, target replaced with the request body
```

The alias and the denied name refer to the same object before and after the write — identical device and inode, with the target's size and SHA-256 changing to those of the submitted body.

Negative controls all behave: a rule added for `/allowed/link` makes the alias return `403`; a user without `Download` does not receive the file; a user without `Modify` cannot write and the target hash is unchanged; a link pointing outside the scope is rejected, so scope containment itself still holds; and the behaviour persists across a restart with the same database.

Reproduced against the real `rawHandler` and `resourcePutHandler` with these controls in place.

## Impact

An authenticated ordinary user can read any file a path rule was meant to deny them, and with `Modify` can replace such a file with arbitrary bytes, provided it is reachable through an in-scope alias and the File Browser process can read or write it. This defeats the confidentiality and integrity guarantees of global and per-user path rules within the user's own scope.

It is not a scope escape. The `ScopedFs` boundary is unaffected, and a link pointing outside the scope is still refused.

## Patches

None. The project is no longer maintained and no fix will ship.

## Workarounds

- Audit each user's scope for symbolic links whose target falls inside a rule-denied path, and remove or repoint them. This is the direct mitigation, since the precondition is the link.
- Where possible, place rule-denied data outside every user scope rather than relying on a deny rule to carve it out from within. Scope containment is enforced against the resolved target; path rules are not.
- Mount volumes into a user's scope with care: restored backups, shared volumes and extracted archives are the realistic sources of a qualifying link.

## Out of scope

The report is explicit about what it does not establish, and this advisory follows it:

- Creation of the required symbolic link through File Browser itself was not demonstrated, and no File Browser API creates one. The link is an out-of-band precondition, which is why attack complexity is rated high.
- No cross-scope access, authentication bypass, administrator privilege escalation, code execution or availability impact is claimed. A link pointing outside the scope was tested and rejected.
- Only raw `GET` and resource `PUT` were exercised. Other handlers share the same checker and are expected to behave the same way, but were not run.
- Windows and macOS were not tested.

## References

- Scope containment against resolved symlink targets, which remains effective: GHSA-239w-m3h6-ch8v
- Lexical rule matching: `rules/rules.go`, `Rule.Matches`
- Symlink resolution without rule context: `files/scoped.go`, `ScopedFs.within`

advisories.summary: Archive downloads hang forever on named pipes
advisories.description:
## Summary

The single-file download handler refuses named pipes, but the directory-archive walker does not:
archiving a directory that contains a FIFO calls `open(2)` on it, which blocks forever when no writer is
attached. The request goroutine and the client connection are pinned indefinitely — there is no timeout,
and context cancellation cannot interrupt a blocking `open(2)`. Repeated requests accumulate pinned
goroutines. The public download handler has the same gap, where it also applies to a share pointing
directly at a named pipe, so the hang is reachable by anonymous visitors holding a public share link.

Verified at v2.63.23, the final release.

## Details

The guard exists at the authenticated entry point only:

```go
// http/raw.go:94-97 (rawHandler)
if files.IsNamedPipe(file.Mode) {
	setContentDisposition(w, r, file)
	return 0, nil
}
```

It was added in [`586d198d`](https://github.com/filebrowser/filebrowser/commit/586d198d) ("fix: fix
hanging when reading a named pipe file", #1155). Two sibling paths reach `Open` without it.

`getFiles` appends every non-directory entry with a live `Open` callback and no entry-type check:

```go
// http/raw.go:136-142
archiveFiles = append(archiveFiles, archives.FileInfo{
	FileInfo:      info,
	NameInArchive: nameInArchive,
	Open: func() (fs.File, error) {
		return d.user.Fs.Open(path)
	},
})
```

`mholt/archives` `openAndCopyFile` then calls `file.Open()` unconditionally, and `open(2)` on a
writer-less FIFO blocks. `archiver.Archive` (`http/raw.go:212`) is passed the request context, but
cancellation cannot interrupt a blocking `open(2)` syscall, so the goroutine never returns even after the
client disconnects.

`publicDlHandler` calls `rawFileHandler` with no guard of its own, so a share pointing directly at a
named pipe hangs on the single-file path too:

```go
// http/public.go:131-138
var publicDlHandler = withHashFile(func(w http.ResponseWriter, r *http.Request, d *data) (int, error) {
	file := d.raw.(*files.FileInfo)
	if !file.IsDir {
		return rawFileHandler(w, r, file)
	}

	return rawDirHandler(w, r, d, file)
})
```

Creating such a share is not prevented: `sharePostHandler` only stats the path
(`http/share.go:159-168`), and `Stat` succeeds on a FIFO without opening it.

## PoC

```bash
BASE=http://127.0.0.1:8099
TOKEN=$(curl -s -X POST $BASE/api/login -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d '{"username":"editor","password":"…"}')

# place a FIFO inside the user's scope (host-side; a user with shell/CLI access to the
# storage tree, or any sync/mount tooling, can create one)
mkdir -p /srv/fb-root/shared/f && echo x > /srv/fb-root/shared/f/normal.txt
mkfifo /srv/fb-root/shared/f/pipe

# archive the directory — request never completes
time curl -s --max-time 15 -o /dev/null -w '%{http_code}\n' \
  "$BASE/api/raw/?files=%2Fshared%2Ff%2F&algo=zip" -H "X-Auth: $TOKEN"
# → curl exits 28 after exactly 15.0s, zero bytes (hang; replayed 2/2)

# anonymous variant: publicly share /shared/f and fetch
#   $BASE/api/public/dl/<hash>/   (archive of the shared dir) — same hang, no auth needed
```

With the FIFO removed, the same archive request returns 200 in ~2 ms. During the hang, concurrent
requests are still served — each hung request pins its own goroutine and connection.

## Impact

Any user with download permission — or an anonymous visitor holding a public share link — can pin one
server goroutine plus one connection per request, with no recovery short of restarting the process.
Scripted repetition accumulates pinned goroutines and connection slots into a denial-of-service
condition.

The named pipe has to be in the served tree already: File Browser's own API cannot create one, so this
requires host-side access to the storage — a shell, a mount, sync tooling, or the command-execution
feature.

## Patches

None. The project is no longer maintained and no fix will ship.

## Workarounds

- Do not serve trees that contain named pipes, sockets or device nodes. A dedicated data volume holding
  only regular files and directories removes the precondition entirely.
- A response timeout on the reverse proxy releases the client's connection, but note that it does **not**
  free the blocked server-side goroutine — only a restart does.

## Out of scope

- **Content disclosure through a FIFO with a live writer.** `openAndCopyFile` copies with
  `io.CopyN(w, fileReader, file.Size())`, and a FIFO's stat size is 0, so the entry is archived as zero
  bytes.
- **The preview endpoint.** `detectType` returns early with `Type: "blob"` for a named pipe
  (`files/file.go:222-226`), so `previewHandler` answers 501 before it can reach `rawFileHandler`.

## References

- [`586d198d`](https://github.com/filebrowser/filebrowser/commit/586d198d) — the named-pipe guard for
  single-file downloads (#1155).

advisories.summary: Deleting another user's shared file leaves their public share link behind
advisories.description:
## Summary

When a file is deleted, File Browser cleans up the public share links that pointed at it — but only
those owned by the user performing the delete. If an administrator, or any other user whose scope
resolves the same path, deletes a file that someone else had publicly shared, the owner's share record
survives. When any file later appears at that path, the old unauthenticated link — original password and
expiry intact — serves the new, unrelated content.

Verified at v2.63.23, the final release. The owner filter on this path was introduced in v2.63.6 by the
fix for GHSA-5ww9-jg6q-38r7.

## Details

The delete handler passes the deleter's user ID into share cleanup:

```go
// http/resource.go:110 (resourceDeleteHandler)
err = d.store.Share.DeleteWithPathPrefix(file.Path, d.user.ID)
```

The Bolt backend then skips every share that is not owned by that user:

```go
// storage/bolt/share.go:93-96 (DeleteWithPathPrefix)
for _, link := range links {
	if link.UserID != userID {
		continue
	}
```

That filter was added in [`0231b7eb`](https://github.com/filebrowser/filebrowser/commit/0231b7eb) to stop
one user from deleting another user's share links through the share-management API. It applies to this
filesystem-event cleanup path as well, so the cleanup now misses exactly the shares that the delete has
invalidated. `withHashFile` resolves `link.Path` lazily on each request (`http/public.go:41-53`), so the
surviving link 404s while the path is absent and serves whatever file appears there next.

## PoC

Two users, `editor` and `admin`, both scoped to `/`.

```bash
BASE=http://127.0.0.1:8099
ED=$(curl -s -X POST $BASE/api/login -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d '{"username":"editor","password":"…"}')
AD=$(curl -s -X POST $BASE/api/login -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d '{"username":"admin","password":"…"}')

# 1. editor creates and publicly shares a file
curl -s -X POST "$BASE/api/resources/x.txt" -H "X-Auth: $ED" --data 'OLD-CONTENT'
HASH=$(curl -s -X POST "$BASE/api/share/x.txt" -H "X-Auth: $ED" -d '{}' | jq -r .hash)
curl -s "$BASE/api/public/dl/$HASH/x.txt"          # → OLD-CONTENT (unauthenticated)

# 2. ADMIN deletes the file
curl -s -o /dev/null -w '%{http_code}\n' -X DELETE "$BASE/api/resources/x.txt" \
  -H "X-Auth: $AD"                                 # → 204

# 3. editor's share record survived the admin's delete
curl -s "$BASE/api/shares" -H "X-Auth: $ED"        # → still lists {"path":"/x.txt",…}

# 4. editor recreates the file with new content
curl -s -X POST "$BASE/api/resources/x.txt" -H "X-Auth: $ED" --data 'NEW-CONTENT'

# 5. the old link serves the NEW file, unauthenticated
curl -s "$BASE/api/public/dl/$HASH/x.txt"          # → NEW-CONTENT   (replayed 2/2)
```

When `editor` deletes her **own** shared file, the share is removed and the recreated file stays private
(404) — confirming the cleanup works only for same-user deletes.

## Impact

Any workflow where a privileged user deletes another user's shared file — admin cleanup, a shared scope —
silently leaves the public link alive. The link later exposes whatever new file appears at that path,
unauthenticated, with no indication to the owner that their link is still live.

## Patches

None. The project is no longer maintained and no fix will ship.

## Workarounds

- Administrators can audit every user's links with `GET /api/shares` and revoke any of them with
  `DELETE /api/share/{hash}`. Do that after deleting a path that belongs to another user.
- Give shares an expiry and a password, so a resurrected link is time-bounded and not anonymously usable.
- Avoid granting several accounts delete permission over one identical scope.

## Out of scope

Share paths are stored relative to the owner's scope (`Path: r.URL.Path` in `sharePostHandler`, resolved
against the owner's filesystem in `withHashFile`). The gap is therefore only reachable when the deleter
and the share owner resolve the *same* path string — in practice, when they hold the same scope. Where
scopes overlap under different roots, the stored path and the deleted path differ, and the prefix query
would not match the other user's share with or without the owner filter.

For the same reason, this advisory does not endorse the reported remediation of dropping the owner filter
outright: that would let one user's delete destroy an unrelated user's share whose scope-relative path
merely happens to collide, re-opening GHSA-5ww9-jg6q-38r7. A correct fix would have to resolve each
candidate share's path through its own owner's scope before deciding.

## References

- GHSA-5ww9-jg6q-38r7 — cross-user share-link deletion; its fix introduced the owner filter on this path.
- GHSA-m8v4-4w34-rrvf — the rename path performs no share cleanup at all.
- GHSA-pp88-jhwj-5qh5 — stale share left by a trailing-slash delete (the same impact class).

advisories.summary: Renaming a shared file leaves the public share link behind
advisories.description:
## Summary

Share records are keyed by path and are cleaned up when the shared path is deleted, but not when it is
renamed. After a shared file is renamed, its share record survives. The link 404s only while the old path
is absent; as soon as any file appears at that path again — the owner re-uploads, another user with
create permission writes there, a hook produces it — the old unauthenticated link, with its original
password and expiry, serves the new and unrelated file.

Verified at v2.63.23, the final release. Every version that has both shares and rename is affected.

## Details

The delete handler removes the shares that its delete invalidated:

```go
// http/resource.go:110 (resourceDeleteHandler)
err = d.store.Share.DeleteWithPathPrefix(file.Path, d.user.ID)
```

The rename branch of `patchAction` deletes thumbnails and moves the file, with no equivalent cleanup:

```go
// http/resource.go:398-423 (patchAction, action == "rename")
	// delete thumbnails
	err = delThumbs(ctx, fileCache, file)
	if err != nil {
		return err
	}

	return fileutils.MoveFile(d.user.Fs, src, dst, d.settings.FileMode, d.settings.DirMode)
```

`resourceDeleteHandler` is the only caller of `DeleteWithPathPrefix` anywhere in the codebase.

`withHashFile` resolves the stored path lazily, on every request (`http/public.go:41-53`): it builds a
`FileInfo` for `link.Path` each time, so the link 404s while the path is missing and serves whatever file
exists there once it reappears. The existence check added to `sharePostHandler`
(`http/share.go:159-168`) only guards the moment the share is created — a rename re-creates the dangling
condition afterwards.

## PoC

```bash
BASE=http://127.0.0.1:8099
TOKEN=$(curl -s -X POST $BASE/api/login -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d '{"username":"user","password":"…"}')

# 1. create and share a file
curl -s -X POST "$BASE/api/resources/a.txt" -H "X-Auth: $TOKEN" --data 'OLD-CONTENT'
HASH=$(curl -s -X POST "$BASE/api/share/a.txt" -H "X-Auth: $TOKEN" -d '{}' | jq -r .hash)

# 2. unauthenticated download works
curl -s "$BASE/api/public/dl/$HASH/a.txt"          # → OLD-CONTENT

# 3. rename the file (no share cleanup on this path)
curl -s -X PATCH "$BASE/api/resources/a.txt?action=rename&destination=%2Fb.txt" \
  -H "X-Auth: $TOKEN"

# 4. link is dormant while the path is absent
curl -s -o /dev/null -w '%{http_code}\n' "$BASE/api/public/dl/$HASH/a.txt"   # → 404

# 5. a new, unrelated file lands at the old path
curl -s -X POST "$BASE/api/resources/a.txt" -H "X-Auth: $TOKEN" --data 'NEW-CONTENT'

# 6. the OLD link now serves the NEW file, unauthenticated
curl -s "$BASE/api/public/dl/$HASH/a.txt"          # → NEW-CONTENT   (replayed 2/2)
```

Sharing a file, **deleting** it and recreating it leaves the share dead (404) — the delete path cleans
up, so the gap is specific to rename.

## Impact

A previously circulated public link silently resurrects and exposes a new, unrelated file that happens to
land at the old path — unauthenticated, under the original link's password and expiry. A user who
re-creates a file under a name they once shared reasonably assumes it is private, while the old link
still serves it. Exploitation is opportunistic rather than directed: the attacker holds an old link and
waits for content to reappear at that path.

## Patches

None. The project is no longer maintained and no fix will ship.

## Workarounds

- Revoke the link by hand after renaming a shared path: list shares with `GET /api/shares` and delete
  with `DELETE /api/share/{hash}`. Administrators see and can revoke every user's shares.
- Give shares an expiry and a password, so a resurrected link is time-bounded and not anonymously usable.

## References

- GHSA-3q2p-72cj-682c — pre-created shares for non-existent paths (the creation-time existence check).
- GHSA-pp88-jhwj-5qh5 — stale share left by a trailing-slash delete (the same impact class, on the delete
  path).
- GHSA-r6pg-pg54-rcr5 — share cleanup on delete matches only the deleter's own shares.

advisories.summary: Concurrent TUS uploads write past the declared Upload-Length
advisories.description:
## Summary

The TUS upload handler enforces the declared `Upload-Length` per request only. Nothing serializes
concurrent `PATCH` requests against a single upload, so two or more PATCHes sent at the same offset all
pass the offset-conflict check before any of them writes, and every body is appended to the file. The
resulting file exceeds its declared length (2× demonstrated), and the upload-completion hook fires for
it. This defeats the per-request bound added in v2.63.19 for GHSA-ffv3-7h97-993q.

Verified at v2.63.23, the final release. The race itself dates to the introduction of TUS in v2.24.0.

## Details

`tusPatchUpload` stats the file and rejects an offset that does not match its size:

```go
// http/tus_handlers.go:237-243
case file.Size != uploadOffset:
	return http.StatusConflict, fmt.Errorf(
		"%s file size doesn't match the provided offset: %d",
		file.RealPath(),
		uploadOffset,
	)
```

then opens the file in append mode and caps the body at the bytes still expected:

```go
// http/tus_handlers.go:245
openFile, err := d.user.Fs.OpenFile(r.URL.Path, os.O_WRONLY|os.O_APPEND, d.settings.FileMode)

// http/tus_handlers.go:265-266
remaining := uploadLength - uploadOffset
bytesWritten, err := io.Copy(openFile, io.LimitReader(r.Body, remaining+1))
```

Two or more concurrent PATCHes at `Upload-Offset: 0` all observe `file.Size == 0` and all pass the
conflict check. `O_APPEND` makes the `Seek` at `:251` a no-op for writes, so every body lands at
end-of-file rather than overwriting. There is no mutex, no offset tracking and no compare-and-swap
anywhere in the stat → check → write window: `UploadCache` records only the declared length. Each winner
that computes `newOffset >= uploadLength` calls `cache.Complete` and fires the `upload` hook:

```go
// http/tus_handlers.go:288-291
if newOffset >= uploadLength {
	cache.Complete(file.RealPath())
	_ = d.RunHook(func() error { return nil }, "upload", r.URL.Path, "", d.user)
}
```

## PoC

Against a stock instance, as a user with create permission:

```bash
# 1. create upload declaring 32 MiB
curl -s -i -X POST "http://127.0.0.1:8099/api/tus/race.bin?override=false" \
  -H "X-Auth: $TOKEN" -H 'Tus-Resumable: 1.0.0' -H 'Upload-Length: 33554432'
# → 201 Created

# 2. fire 8 concurrent PATCHes at offset 0, each with a 32 MiB body
for i in 1 2 3 4 5 6 7 8; do
  curl -s -o /dev/null -w '%{http_code}\n' -X PATCH \
    "http://127.0.0.1:8099/api/tus/race.bin" \
    -H "X-Auth: $TOKEN" -H 'Tus-Resumable: 1.0.0' \
    -H 'Upload-Offset: 0' -H 'Content-Type: application/offset+octet-stream' \
    --data-binary @chunk32m.bin &
done; wait
```

Observed over 2 independent runs: two PATCHes return `204 No Content` with
`Upload-Offset: 33554432`, the rest `409`; the file on disk is 67,108,864 bytes — exactly 2× the declared
length — and the upload hook fired.

The sequential bound still holds: a sequential over-length PATCH returns `413` and the file is truncated;
a sequential PATCH after completion returns `404`. Only the concurrent path bypasses it.

## Impact

An authenticated user with create permission can write a multiple of the declared `Upload-Length` to
disk — N × `Upload-Length` for N racing requests — so the size the server accepted for an upload is not
the size it stores. The completion hook also fires for a file that violates its declared length, which
can mislead operator-configured downstream processing.

## Patches

None. The project is no longer maintained and no fix will ship.

## Workarounds

- Serialize or rate-limit `PATCH /api/tus/*` per user at the reverse proxy, so concurrent PATCHes against
  one upload cannot reach the handler together.
- Bound the storage File Browser writes to with a filesystem quota or a dedicated volume, so an
  over-length file cannot affect the rest of the host.

## Out of scope

Disk exhaustion as such is not treated as the impact here. File Browser has no maximum upload size and no
storage quota, so a user holding Create or Modify permission is already authorized to write files of
arbitrary size within their own scope — the same position taken in GHSA-ffv3-7h97-993q. What this report
establishes is that the declared-length contract can be broken, not a new capacity to fill the disk, and
the severity is rated on that basis. Per-user quotas remain an unimplemented feature request (#711,
#2090, #2179, #2361).

## References

- GHSA-ffv3-7h97-993q — the per-request `Upload-Length` enforcement that this race defeats.

advisories.summary: Expired JWTs accepted under proxy auth with a custom logout page
advisories.description:
## Summary

Under proxy authentication with a non-default `auth.logoutPage`, File Browser waives the JWT expiration inside its shared authentication middleware. An expired but validly signed token therefore keeps authenticating every protected route, administrative ones included, and can be exchanged for a fresh token at `/api/renew`, so a token stolen before it expired stays usable indefinitely. Reported against v2.63.2; introduced in v2.50.0 and verified through v2.63.21.

## Details

In `http/auth.go`, `renewableErr` treats `jwt.ErrTokenExpired` as renewable whenever the auth method is proxy and the logout page is non-default, and `withUser` consults it on every request instead of only on a renewal path:

```go
	token, err := request.ParseFromRequest(r, &extractor{}, keyFunc, request.WithClaims(&tk), request.WithParser(p))
	if (err != nil || !token.Valid) && !renewableErr(err, d) {
		return http.StatusUnauthorized, nil
	}
```

The middleware then loads the user named by the expired claims and continues. `withAdmin` is layered on `withUser`, so administrative routes inherit the behavior, and `renewHandler` — also built on `withUser` — hands out a new token.

Waiving the expiration is intentional: under proxy authentication the trusted proxy, not the token, owns the session lifetime (see #3884, which for the same reason disables the frontend idle timer in this configuration). The defect is that the waiver was granted on the strength of the token alone, without checking that the proxy still asserts that identity.

## PoC

Preconditions:

- File Browser uses proxy authentication.
- `auth.logoutPage` is configured to a non-default value.
- The attacker holds a previously valid signed token. Its permissions bound the impact.
- Neither JWT forgery nor a bypass of the trusted proxy is required.

Steps:

1. Start an instance with proxy authentication, a non-default logout page, and `tokenExpirationTime=1s` for an accelerated test.
2. Log in through the trusted proxy header as an administrator test account and keep the issued token.
3. Wait for the configured token lifetime to elapse.
4. Request a protected raw file with `X-Auth: <expired token>`. It returns `200` with the protected content and `X-Renew-Token: true`.
5. Request `/api/settings` with the same expired token. It returns `200`.
6. Request `/api/renew` with the same expired token. It returns `200` and a new token.

## Impact

In the affected configuration, JWT expiration cannot end a session. A token captured before it expired continues to read protected data with the permissions it carries — administrative settings when it belongs to an administrator — and can be refreshed indefinitely.

## Patches

Fixed in v2.63.22. The expiration is now waived only when the configured proxy header still names the user the token was issued for, which the trusted proxy asserts on any genuine request; an expired token presented on its own, or alongside a different identity, is rejected with `401`.

## Workarounds

Leave `auth.logoutPage` at its default value, which disables the waiver entirely and restores ordinary token expiration.

## References

- Fix: https://github.com/filebrowser/filebrowser/commit/72faf6dd3c85628e332d3e567124b86708ce2695
- Pull request: https://github.com/filebrowser/filebrowser/pull/6053

advisories.summary: Recursive copy, rename and delete ignore rules denying descendants
advisories.description:
## Summary

File Browser's path rules can deny a descendant while leaving its parent allowed. Recursive copy, rename and delete authorize only the root of the operation and then process the whole subtree, so an authenticated non-administrator can copy or rename an allowed parent to read denied descendants at the new location, or delete the parent to destroy them. Reported against v2.63.2 and verified at v2.63.21.

## Details

`http/resource.go` checks the root of the operation only. `resourcePatchHandler` authorizes the two endpoints of a copy or rename:

```go
	if !d.Check(src) || !d.Check(dst) {
		return http.StatusForbidden, nil
	}
```

and `resourceDeleteHandler` resolves its target through `files.NewFileInfo`, whose checker validates that one path. The recursive work then runs with no checker at all:

```go
	case "copy":
		...
		return fileutils.Copy(d.user.Fs, src, dst, d.settings.FileMode, d.settings.DirMode)
```

```go
		err = d.RunHook(func() error {
			return d.user.Fs.RemoveAll(r.URL.Path)
		}, "delete", r.URL.Path, "", d.user)
```

`fileutils.CopyDir`, `fileutils.MoveFile` and `RemoveAll` walk the tree directly, so every descendant is copied, moved or removed regardless of the rules. Everywhere else the rules are applied per path: listings drop denied entries (`files.FileInfo.readListing`), direct access returns 403 (`files.NewFileInfo`), and the archive download walker checks each descendant (`getFiles` in `http/raw.go`).

## PoC

Preconditions:

- The attacker is an authenticated non-administrator with the relevant file-operation permission on the parent directory.
- A rule denies one or more descendants while leaving the parent allowed.
- The destination of the copy or rename is allowed.

Steps:

1. Deny `/copy-src/secret`, `/rename-src/secret` and `/delete-src/secret`, leave the three parent directories accessible, and place a marker file in each denied directory.
2. As the restricted user, request each denied descendant through the resource API. All three return `403`.
3. `PATCH /api/resources/copy-src/?action=copy&destination=/dst` returns `200`, and the marker is readable at its new path.
4. `PATCH /api/resources/rename-src/?action=rename&destination=/moved` returns `200`, and the marker is readable at its new path.
5. `DELETE /api/resources/delete-src/` returns `204`, and the denied marker file no longer exists.

## Impact

An authenticated user holding ordinary create, rename or delete permission can read, relocate or destroy files the rules deny them, defeating rule-based isolation for confidentiality and integrity alike.

## Patches

Fixed in v2.63.22. Copy, rename and delete now walk the source tree — and the location that tree would land on — before mutating anything, and reject the whole operation with `403` if any path is denied. The walk consults the rules only: hiding dotfiles is a display preference, and must not stop a user from moving a directory that contains one.

## Workarounds

None. Until you can upgrade, withhold create, rename and delete permission from users whose rules deny descendants of directories they may otherwise operate on.

## References

- Fix: https://github.com/filebrowser/filebrowser/commit/72faf6dd3c85628e332d3e567124b86708ce2695
- Pull request: https://github.com/filebrowser/filebrowser/pull/6053

advisories.summary: File checksum disclosure via /api/resources endpoint bypassing Perm.Download check
advisories.description:
## Summary

Incomplete fix of CVE-2026-35606: the /api/resources checksum branch still reads the full file and returns its digest without a Perm.Download check, so a user provisioned with Perm.Download=false gets a file-content hash oracle. It does not defeat scope/path authorization; it bypasses only the Download permission, yielding a content-hash oracle rather than plaintext. Confirmed at HEAD b7dc392838f11d188f0bc0f2a1a99fad3f7dca03.

## The defect

CVE-2026-35606 was that /api/resources returned file content while bypassing Perm.Download. The fix (PR #5891, v2.63.1) gated the content-returning paths (changed the hardcoded Content: true to Content: d.user.Perm.Download, and added a 202 guard to the raw-byte X-Encoding branch). The same handler has a third full-file-reading path, the ?checksum= branch, which reads the entire file to compute a digest and returns it; it was not given a Perm.Download check.

http/resource.go, resourceGetHandler, the checksum branch (around lines 69-79):

```go
if checksum := r.URL.Query().Get("checksum"); checksum != "" {
    err := file.Checksum(checksum)   // reads the whole file into the hash (files/file.go:170-207)
    ...
    return renderJSON(w, r, file)    // returns the digest in the checksums map
}
```

resourceGetHandler (withUser) has no Perm.Download check at the top. The three sibling read paths do guard it: raw.go:85 (`if !d.user.Perm.Download { return http.StatusAccepted, nil }`), preview.go:39, and subtitle.go:18. The checksum branch does not.

## Attacker model and impact

An authenticated low-privilege user provisioned with Perm.Download=false (a first-class supported permission, the exact configuration CVE-2026-35606 is written against). GET /api/resources/<path>?checksum=sha256 (also md5/sha1/sha512) with X-Auth returns the file digest. This is a Download-gate bypass yielding a file-content hash oracle: confirm known or guessed content, detect changes over time, or brute-force low-entropy files offline. It is broader than CVE-2026-35606 in that it hashes any file type of any size, with no text-only restriction and no 10 MB detectType cap. It does not defeat the scope/path authorization (only same-scope files).

Proof of concept: as a user with Perm.Download=false, GET /api/resources/<readable-path>?checksum=sha256 with a valid X-Auth token; the sha256 digest is returned.

## Verification

Source-verified at HEAD: the checksum branch calls file.Checksum with no Perm.Download check, while raw.go:85 guards the same permission. I did not run a live File Browser.

## Suggested fix

Add `if !d.user.Perm.Download { return http.StatusAccepted, nil }` ahead of the checksum branch in resourceGetHandler, matching the raw/preview/subtitle siblings.

## Tooling

I used AI assistance while investigating, but I read the checksum branch (confirming no Perm.Download check) and raw.go (confirming the sibling guards it) myself at HEAD, so the inconsistency is source-verified.

advisories.summary: Out-of-scope file deletion via symlink-following delete in TUS upload-cache eviction
advisories.description:
## Summary
A scoped File Browser user holding only `Perm.Create` can cause the server (running with broader privileges) to delete an arbitrary file **outside the user's scope** — including other tenants' data or the application's own `filebrowser.db`. The default in-memory TUS upload cache registers in-progress uploads under their absolute on-disk path and, on TTL expiry, deletes them with a raw `os.Remove(item.Key())` that bypasses File Browser's `ScopedFs` scope guard entirely. By swapping an ancestor directory of a registered upload for a symlink during the cache TTL window, the attacker redirects the delete to an out-of-scope target.

## Root Cause
When `redisCacheUrl` is empty (the default — `cmd/root.go:93,183-184`), `newMemoryUploadCache` is used. A TUS `POST` registers the upload under its absolute `RealPath`: `cache.Register(file.RealPath(), len)` (`http/tus_handlers.go:113`), where `RealPath` (afero `BasePathFs.RealPath`) is a purely **lexical** `filepath.Clean(filepath.Join(base, name))` with **no `EvalSymlinks`**. When the entry is not completed within `uploadCacheTTL` (3 minutes), the ttlcache eviction callback runs a raw `os.Remove(item.Key())` on a background goroutine (`http/upload_cache_memory.go:41-45`). This is the only request-reachable filesystem mutation in the codebase that never routes through `ScopedFs`/`guard()`/`within()`. Because `os.Remove` resolves symlinks in the **parent directories** of its argument, swapping an ancestor of the frozen key for an escaping symlink causes an out-of-scope file to be deleted.

## Impact
- **I:H / A:H** — deletion of an attacker-chosen file/directory outside the user's scope (other tenants' data, or the single-file `./filebrowser.db` → outage). Runs silently on a background goroutine (only a `fmt.Printf`), no error surfaced.
- **S:C** — impact escapes the user's scope authority. No `Perm.Delete` is required.
The precondition (an out-of-band escaping symlink under the scope, arriving via the same chrooted SFTP/rsync/mounted-volume channel) is identical to the threat model of CVE-2026-54094 → CVE-2026-55667, which the project treats as in-scope; File Browser exposes no symlink API.

## Proof of Concept
```
# 1. Create a real in-scope dir and start a TUS upload named after the target file, no body:
POST /api/tus/d/target.db      Upload-Length: 10
# 2. Within the 3-minute TTL, out-of-band (SFTP/rsync/mounted volume):
rm -rf d && ln -s /srv/users/victim d
# 3. Wait for eviction: os.Remove("<scope>/d/target.db") follows the symlinked parent
#    -> deletes /srv/users/victim/target.db. No Perm.Delete, default config.
```

## Attack Chain
1. **Entry** — Action: `Perm.Create` user sends `POST /api/tus/d/target.db` (`Upload-Length` set, no body); `d` is a real in-scope dir. Guard: `tusPostHandler` `Perm.Create && d.Check` (`http/tus_handlers.go:43`). Bypass proof: only Create needed; `d.Check` is a rule/hidden-dotfile check, not a symlink/scope guard.
2. **OpenFile guard** — Action: `d.user.Fs.OpenFile("d/target.db", O_CREATE|O_WRONLY)` (`tus_handlers.go:88`). Guard: `ScopedFs.guard()`/`within()`. Bypass proof: `d` is a genuine in-scope directory at this instant, so `within()` legitimately passes and the file is created. (The direct-register-through-symlink variant IS blocked here — if `d` is already a symlink, `guard()` returns `ErrPermission` before `cache.Register` — which is why the parent-swap TOCTOU is the working vector.)
3. **Register absolute key** — Action: `cache.Register(file.RealPath(), len)` (`tus_handlers.go:113`) freezes the absolute lexical key `<root>/<scope>/d/target.db`. Guard: none. Bypass proof: `RealPath` = `filepath.Clean(filepath.Join(base,name))`, no `EvalSymlinks`; the key is stored raw and never re-validated. `tusPostHandler` doesn't call `keepUploadActive`, so with no PATCH the entry simply expires.
4. **Parent swap (TOCTOU)** — Action: within the 3-min TTL, out-of-band `rm -rf d && ln -s /srv/users/victim d`. Guard: none — nothing re-checks the cached key. Bypass proof: File Browser never observes or re-validates the swap.
5. **Sink** — Action: ttlcache `OnEviction` (`EvictionReasonExpired`) → `os.Remove("<root>/<scope>/d/target.db")` (`http/upload_cache_memory.go:44`). Guard: NONE — raw stdlib delete, no `ScopedFs`/`within()`/`d.Check`. Bypass proof: `os.Remove` (unlink) resolves the symlinked parent `d`, deleting `/srv/users/victim/target.db`.
6. **Impact** — out-of-scope file/DB deletion; both `ScopedFs` and `Perm.Delete` bypassed.

## Bypass Evidence
- The CVE-2026-55667 fix commit `64511ce` (`git show --name-only`) touches only `files/scoped.go`, `files/file_test.go`, `http/resource_test.go`; it adds `guard()` to `ScopedFs.Remove`/`RemoveAll` (`files/scoped.go:194-206`). It never touches `http/upload_cache_memory.go`.
- `os.Remove(item.Key())` at `upload_cache_memory.go:44` is the only `os.Remove` in `http/`+`files/` and never enters `ScopedFs`; `git log v2.63.15..HEAD -- http/upload_cache_memory.go` is empty (never fixed).
- Local probe: `os.Remove("/tmp/rmtest/link_parent/victim.txt")` with `link_parent -> /tmp/rmtest/outside` deleted the out-of-scope `victim.txt` — confirming `os.Remove` follows a symlinked parent.
- Redis backend does `client.Del` only (no FS delete), so the bug is specific to the default in-memory cache.

## Dedup — Distinct unfixed variant, NOT a duplicate of CVE-2026-55667
CVE-2026-55667 (GHSA-fmm7-x4gx-8jhr) is out-of-scope deletion via symlink-following `ScopedFs.RemoveAll` in upload **failure-cleanup**, fixed by adding `guard()` to `ScopedFs.Remove/RemoveAll`. This finding is a **different sink** (raw `os.Remove`), **different file** (`http/upload_cache_memory.go` vs `files/scoped.go`/`http/resource.go`), **different trigger** (asynchronous ttlcache eviction 3 min later vs synchronous during the POST), and is **unfixed** — the CVE-2026-55667 fix cannot reach a stdlib `os.*` call. Separate sink → separate fix → separate advisory.

## Affected Versions
`>= 2.57.0, <= 2.63.18` — the eviction sink was introduced in commit `08d7a15` (first released in v2.57.0) and is present unchanged on the latest release tag v2.63.18 and on HEAD; no fix on main. Default (in-memory) upload cache only; not Redis.

## Suggested Fix
Route eviction deletes through the scoped filesystem (or re-validate `item.Key()` against the user's scope via `within()` before `os.Remove`), or hold the open file handle and delete by descriptor rather than by path.

---
Reported by **zx (Jace)** — GitHub: @manus-use

advisories.summary: Access rule bypass via case-variant and Windows-separator paths
advisories.description:
## Summary

File Browser's access rules are written as `/`-separated, case-sensitive virtual paths, and the rule
checker compares them literally. The filesystem resolves the same strings with host semantics, so
the two layers disagree about which file a path names. An authenticated user could exploit that
disagreement to reach a file an administrator had denied, while staying inside their own scope.

There are two independent forms. On a case-insensitive filesystem — NTFS, macOS APFS/HFS+ by
default, and NTFS/exFAT/CIFS mounts under Linux — a case-variant of the denied name resolves to the
same file but matches no rule. On Windows, a backslash is a path separator that the filesystem
resolves but the rule checker treated as an ordinary character.

Reported against 2.63.18 and verified over the whole 2.x line up to and including 2.63.20.

## Details

`rules.Rule.Matches` in `rules/rules.go` performed case-sensitive equality and prefix comparisons on
the raw path:

```go
func (r *Rule) Matches(path string) bool {
	if path == r.Path {
		return true
	}
	prefix := r.Path
	if prefix != "/" && !strings.HasSuffix(prefix, "/") {
		prefix += "/"
	}
	return strings.HasPrefix(path, prefix)
}
```

`data.Check` in `http/data.go` handed it the path exactly as received, and the handlers then passed
that same path to the user's filesystem.

For the backslash form, `afero.BasePathFs.RealPath` resolves the path with
`filepath.Clean(filepath.Join(bpath, name))`, which collapses `\..\` on Windows. So
`/allow\..\Secret.txt` matched no rule for `/Secret.txt` and still opened it. gorilla/mux's
`cleanPath` only cleans forward slashes, so the sequence reached the handler intact. The
`destination=` and `files=` query parameters were affected in the same way.

Verification also surfaced a broader instance the report did not cover: the server passed the rule
checker paths it had built itself. `afero.Walk` and `filepath.Join` emit backslashes on Windows, so
`resourceGetRecursiveHandler` in `http/resource.go` and `getFiles` in `http/raw.go` called `Check`
with OS-separated paths. On Windows, no rule — plain path or regular expression — could match a
nested entry in a recursive listing or a download-as-archive request.

## PoC

Preconditions: File Browser on Windows or another case-insensitive filesystem; a normal
authenticated user whose scope contains `/Secret.txt`; an administrator deny rule for the exact path
`/Secret.txt`.

1. Create a file named `Secret.txt`.
2. Add a deny rule for the normal user `test` for the exact path `/Secret.txt`.
3. Log in as `test` and request the canonical path. File Browser rejects the request.
4. Change only the filename casing and send the request again. The response returns the contents of
   `Secret.txt`.
5. The mixed-separator variant, with an existing `allow` directory: request
   `/allow\..\Secret.txt`. On Windows this path resolves back to `Secret.txt` while the rule checker
   evaluates the uncanonicalized string.

## Impact

An ordinary authenticated user can bypass administrator-defined access rules within their own scope.
Depending on the permissions they hold, that means unauthorized disclosure, modification, deletion,
copying, or public sharing of files the administrator explicitly denied. It does not grant access
outside the user's scope.

## Patches

Fixed in v2.63.21 by https://github.com/filebrowser/filebrowser/pull/6045.

Paths are now canonicalized with the host's own separator before every rule decision and at each
point an external path enters, so the rule checker and the filesystem always agree on which file a
path names. This is a no-op on POSIX, where a backslash is a legal filename character and remains
one. Path rules are additionally matched case-insensitively when the filesystem is
case-insensitive, detected by probing the server root at startup rather than inferred from the
operating system — macOS can be formatted case-sensitively, and Linux commonly serves a
case-insensitive mount. Regular-expression rules are unchanged: an administrator-authored pattern
means what it says, and `(?i)` remains the opt-in.

## Workarounds

None. Upgrade to v2.63.21.

## Out of scope

Windows recognizes further aliases for the same file that this fix deliberately does not chase:
NTFS alternate data streams (`/Secret.txt::$DATA`), Win32's stripping of trailing dots and spaces
(`/Secret.txt.`), and 8.3 short names (`SECRET~1.TXT`) on volumes where short-name generation is
enabled. APFS and HFS+ additionally normalize Unicode, so composed and decomposed spellings of the
same name are aliases there.

Rejecting the characters involved would be an incomplete denylist — the 8.3 alias contains no
special character at all — and the complete fix, resolving each path segment's true on-disk name on
every request, costs a directory read per segment and cannot work for paths that are being created.
Administrators who rely on access rules on Windows should disable 8.3 name generation on the served
volume (`fsutil 8dot3name set 1`).

## References

- Fix and regression tests: https://github.com/filebrowser/filebrowser/pull/6045
